On Monday a new extraordinary parliamentary session begins, for the endorsement of further legislation undertaken by Bucharest as part of the recovery and resilience facility. The Chamber of Deputies will discuss a new bill on the integrity of civil servants and legislation already endorsed by the Senate, as the first chamber notified. The Senate’s agenda includes the 2026-2030 National Strategy and Action Plan on Biodiversity Conservation. Of the draft laws that need to be endorsed by the end of this month as milestones in the PNNR, an agreement backed by a parliamentary majority is yet to be identified with respect to the public sector salary bill. ALERT Romania is facing one of the worst drought periods in recent years, with the Danube water flow dropping to almost 3 times below the multi-annual average for the month, close to its all-time low, according to the Romanian Waters Agency. Authorities are taking emergency measures to keep the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant in operation, as the Danube water flow is extremely low and experts warn the nuclear power plant can barely operate for another 4-5 days. Electricity demand is on the rise due to the high temperatures, and Transelectrica estimates a peak of around 7,800 megawatts next week. The government has declared a nation-wide state of alert for the month of August, because of the fall in the electricity output entailed by the drought. The caretaker PM Ilie Bolojan announced he had talks with Ukraine’s deputy PM and minister of energy, Denys Shmyhal, about support for Romania in high electricity demand periods. Bucharest is also discussing with partners in Bulgaria and Greece to increase imports. Ilie Bolojan added that all national production facilities were requested to work at full capacity so as to preserve the balance in the national energy system. He also called for voluntary electricity saving, especially in the evening. WEATHER Meteorologists have issued several extreme heat warnings valid until Tuesday morning. A code red warning will be in effect in western and northwestern Romania. The highs will reach 40 degrees Celsius, with a temperature-humidity index (ITU) above the critical 80-unit threshold. A code orange warning has also been issued for the north and west of the country, with highs of 38 degrees Celsius, while a code yellow warning will be in place in the northeast, east, centre and southwest. Elsewhere in the country, the weather remains hot, with increasing thermal discomfort and highs between 27 and 40 degrees Celsius. DRONE The defence ministry’s radar surveillance system Sunday detected an aerial target near the river border with Ukraine. Two Romanian Air Force F-16 aircraft from the 86th Borcea Air Base took off to monitor the situation. The target moved for approximately 20 minutes above the territorial waters and along the Danube’s Sulina branch, in the national airspace, then it left the territory of Romania towards Ukraine, where it was shot down by the Ukrainian forces. Drone fragments fell close to ​​the village of Periprava, on a field approx. 1 km from the border. No casualties or damages were reported. The National Military Command Centre instructed the General Inspectorate for Emergencies to alert the public in Tulcea County via a RO-Alert message. At the end of last week, 3 drones that illegally entered the national airspace were shot down in three consecutive days by Romanian Air Force F-16 aircraft. BACCALAUREATE In Romania, the second session of this year’s baccalaureate exam begins on Monday with the oral Romanian literature test, and continues next week with the other skills assessment tests. The written tests are scheduled to begin on August 10, and the first results are expected on August 18. The education ministry is yet to announce the number of candidates who have enrolled in the so-called autumn session. Last year, there were over 30,000 candidates, and the pass rate was almost 32%. ROMA HOLOCAUST On National Roma Holocaust Memorial Day (Samudaripen) marked on Sunday, the foreign ministry paid tribute to the memory of the Roma Holocaust victims. On August 2, 1944, 82 years ago, around 3,000 Roma at the Auschwitz-Birkenau camp were killed by the Nazi regime. Over 500,000 Roma were killed in Europe during World War II. The foreign ministry supports national and international initiatives to promote education, research and commemoration of the Roma genocide. The institution also voices concern over the proliferation of hate speech against members of the Roma community, especially online, and reaffirms the need to fight discrimination and extremist actions of an ethnic or racial nature. The Roma are the largest ethnic minority group in Europe. Of the approximately 12 million Roma people in Europe, around 6 million are EU citizens or residents. Many Roma in the EU are still victims of prejudice and social exclusion, despite clear regulations on discrimination in all EU member states, according to the European Commission. RATING The CFA Romania head Adrian Codirlaşu believes that Romania narrowly avoided a downgrade in its country rating, and the Fitch report indicates a worsening of the economic outlook. He argues the decision to keep the rating in place was possible because the government proved it can keep public spending in check, but warns that the lack of reforms, the risk of losing EU funds and a possible return to high deficits keep the economy in a vulnerable situation. President Nicuşor Dan welcomed the Fitch Agency report, which reconfirms Romania’s financial stability. The agency announced it maintains Romania’s sovereign rating at BBB-, with a negative outlook. Citing the deterioration of public finances, political uncertainty and risks regarding the implementation of reforms, Fitch warns, however, that without further fiscal consolidation measures, there is a significant risk of the rating being downgraded to “junk”. The financial rating agency estimates that in 2026 the budget deficit will be 5.9% of GDP, and economic growth will be 0.6%. On August 7, Moody’s is also scheduled to release its rating report for Romania. Then it got hit by floods A placard mocking the BJP's lotus symbol during a protest in Pune on July 24. | Scroll Staff On a chilly morning in December 1989, Romanian President Nicolae Ceaușescu stepped onto the balcony of the Communist Party headquarters in Bucharest to deliver a speech. The crowd was full with people holding up carrying massive pictures of the version of him, and of his wife Elena. Ceaușescu was very particular about how he looked on photographs – a team made sure wrinkles were removed and any photo looked perfectly staged. The widely circulated large posters of him had him in his 40s, people in Romania marveled at how his official posters refused to age. Like an unfortunate analogy for South Indian movie stardom, the crowd waving posters of the yesteryear blockbuster, facing an arthritic live version. At first, the event seemed to be going alright. There were the usual celebratory chants, revolutionary slogans being waved on large red banners, the perfected dictatorship-style choreographed clapping lining the speech. Then something unexpected happened. Someone booed, then another person booed, and another. Within seconds the entire crowd burst into aggressive heckling. The leader, so used to complete obedience and speeches peppered with the chant “Ceaușescu și poporul” (Ceaușescu and the people) was suddenly caught on camera with an expression his pre-Photoshop airbrushed images hadn’t prepared people for. He looked stunned and helpless, repeatedly asking the crowd to calm down. In this photograph from December 21, 1989, a television screen shows former Romanian communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu delivering his last public speech from the balcony of the Romanian Communist Party Headquarters’ in Bucharest. Credit: AFP. His wife, similarly used to her de facto role as the second in command, had no luck trying to get people to quiet down. A row of cronies standing alongside on the balcony seemed likewise shocked, as a feared leader seemed to suddenly fail to instill dread in the people. The national broadcaster’s television cameras covering the speech quickly turned the lens away from the jeering crowds and up towards the sky. Ceaușescu had wielded near-complete power over the state and its institutions. The majority of the country’s population had known no leader other than him. There were massive banners and large cutouts of him in city squares, even photos in schools and factories. There were regular television missives from him, typically with him facing the camera directly, often taking only pre-selected questions. He never did direct, unscripted engagements with journalists. All mainstream media was carefully managed, information that the people got from the government were presented as coming from Comrade Ceaușescu – factories existed because of him, agricultural successes came from his guidance, technological achievements were from his genius. The common term of reference for this Eastern Bloc Vishwaguru was “Geniul Carpaților” – The Genius of the Carpathians. The region was in disarray, but unlike Poland or Czechoslovakia there was no functional opposition in Romania. There was no problem with organised and disaffected regional minorities like in Yugoslavia. The state security apparatus, the Securitate, was extremely effective and feared. The standard process was to quickly prosecute and quell any dissenters as enemies of the state. Anyone of institutional significance – the army, bureaucracy, judiciary – had been vetted for loyalty to Ceaușescu and the party. And yet, within a day of that catastrophic speech, he was reduced to a deposed prisoner. The downfall of Ceaușescu was among the most unexpected and rapid falls from power in the history of modern politics. While the shock of booing was a massive trigger, the turning point moment of his downfall was when the television cameras turned away from the crowd and up towards the sky. That moment broadcast fear. The past fortnight, the streets of the capital in India saw chants of protestors describing Prime Minister Narendra Modi as a coward who hid from the press, people openly asking for his resignation. But even with pliant television, turning the camera from the crowd to the sky was no longer possible. Not only was the fear of the genius leader and his apparatus struck down, even the unwritten rules of liberal civility were out of the window. Full-frontal verbal assaults that were typically inflicted on the Opposition by the ruling party were now being dished out by protestors taking aim at everything that was sacred to the leader and establishment’s image, things that had been built up over years of branding. For his 56-inch chest, protesters asked that he “tighten his bra”, for his picture-perfect photoshoots, protesters asked that he spruce up the lipstick, his chaiwala claims, once a marker of his connection to the ground reality of India, became a fodder for a flood of quickly assembled, handheld posters. In a country where even “liking” the wrong social media message had been grounds for arrest, it felt like all bets were off as the internet eagerly awaited the next hilarious meme. The strong arm of the khaki vardi had seemingly ceased to scare students who stayed upright against swinging sticks of the Delhi Police, as they were also immune to the potential threats of sanskari lynch-happy mobs. This was a true fight or flight moment. Supporters of the Cockroach Janata Party celebrate after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned, in New Delhi on July 25. Credit: Reuters. The information environment and the shock event It could have gone the Tiananmen Square way. The lathis could have turned into armoured cars. But there was a problem. The more aggressive the media control, the more even the smallest bit of dissent could kill all semblance of narrative control. Crowds can be cleared out, but the memes were out. The information environment had been changed. Insulting the prime minister had suddenly become cool and, as the Bharatiya Janata Party knew very well when it stuck the pejorative “Pappu” Rahul Gandhi, it takes years to roll back the butt of a joke. Within a few days, Modi had bent to the will of the student agitators, accepting all their demands for and conveying his acquiescence on the media platform they decided to use most aggressively to attack him – Instagram. Regimes that thrive on the belief that they have permanently convinced their people that resistance is futile do not deal well with shocks. In most cases, the information environment is critical in determining if the boiling point will cause an explosion. In the run-up to the events that defined the French Revolution in 1789, for instance, there was discontent brewing and a range of other problems with the flailing finances of Louis XVI’s regime. But the days leading up to the shock event, the storming of the Bastille by common people in Paris, saw a flood of insecurities surface and detonate. The information environment at the time included newspapers and official royal missives, but these had little impact on the crowds. Instead, it was cafe gossip, tales from travelers, and unverified pamphlets that got around a lot faster. The throne of King Louis Philippe is burned in Bastille Palace during the French revolution of 1848. Credit: Nathaniel Currier, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. A range of stories with dubious sources suddenly hit a nerve – the aristocracy was plotting a famine against common people, banquets at the palace were mocking the movement, foreign mercenaries were being organised to attack common Parisians, the king was sending troops to dissolve the national assembly, and of course, Queen Marie Antoinette was asking the people with no access to bread to eat cake instead. The rest is a history podcast. A few decades later, it was Japan’s turn to lose an information war in what was a far stranger situation than the Paris uprising. For centuries, Japan had a remarkably stable Shogunate, and while the forced entry of Western trade had shaken it up, the relationship between the people and the state remained solidly hierarchical, with feudal lords and the Samurai class on top, and the rural peasantry largely living on subsistence. In 1867, Japan had a movement, named after the slogan that came to define it, Ee Ja Nai Ka movement, which did not feature wholesale assault on the leadership or security forces, but featured a lot of people behaving wildly in groups and breaking social norms of good behaviour. For some context, the worst lawlessness to come out of the movement was some looting of alcohol – levels of bad behavior that would probably not be worth talking about anyplace other than Japan. Throughout 1867, especially in the belt between Kyoto and Osaka, common people, mostly peasants, stormed the streets screaming “Ee Ja Nai Ka”, literally meaning “What the hell?” or “Why not?” The immediate driver was rumours that there were sacred talismans falling from the sky and that they were a sign of change. But the deeper meaning was a “to hell with it” take in which people suddenly started to believe that anything could happen, that the old rules no longer applied, and well, one may as well party. People who forget that protests can often feel like a carnival were reminded in Delhi that not everyone is out calling for armed insurrection against the regime – many protesters are quite simply having a nihilistic moment in which they plan to share the frenzy of the mob as a simple, even enjoyable act of resistance. In this form, people went into carnivalesque frenzies across Japan’s towns, abandoning work in the fields, running out in wild costumes and spontaneously dancing on the streets, setting up ad-hoc costume parades, all of which would be considered anywhere between inappropriate and unhinged. The dancing and parades had clear political undertones – cross dressing, as well as the young dressing as old to undermine gender and hierarchy codes, with the chant of “Ee Ja Nai Ka” used as a refrain for “Old Rules Don’t Matter” rather than the literal translation. A scene depicting dancing during the “Ee ja nai ka” movement. Credit: Kawanabe Kyōsai, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Attempts by merchants and the feudal establishment to stop these and bring workers back to the fields failed. At the time, Japan had a highly organised and strictly hierarchical system of feudal lords, with a range of institutionalised systems in place to stop rebellion. One was called gonin-gumi. It was a small set of households, typically five, ordered like a neighborhood association, in which each household was responsible for the behavior of others. But it was not like a shiny happy self-help group: it was a means of keeping strict order, acting like a spy agency similar to Ceaușescu neighborhood-level surveillance through the Romanian Securitate. It enabled tax collection through the constant threat of collective punishment. The authorities put out several decrees banning the dancing, and tried at first to ignore these events. Eventually, they tried to repress the events, or threaten punishments. Word about these talismans and various forms of divine intervention, all of which were taken as signs for people to run wild, came from unverifiable sources such as travelling merchants, entertainers, or pilgrims. On the other hand, formal sources such as missives from local officials or from the Shogunate were expressly ignored. The two events were very distinct in that the French Revolution crescendoed very quickly, while the Ee Ja Nai Ka was a distributed, disorganised slow burn. Although these shock events were effectively rebellions in that they acted against orders, the French Revolution had clear protagonists and antagonists whereas Ee Ja Nai Ka was more of a catharsis. Neither event had a well-defined leadership, nor a locus of control with clear instructions or goals. Both led to change, although not immediate. Both events led to concessions for the participants in the events and they were overwhelmingly not prosecuted. It did not end well for the masters of either society. The protests did not immediately depose them – the Shogun remained in power for several months after, while the much-weakened French king continued to rule for three years. But it eventually also ended badly for the close quarter groups of the leadership. As the Shogunate ended, so did the superior place of the Samurai, the class that aligned most closely with the Shogunate. It went from being on top of the social hierarchy to poverty and scraping the bottom. For the aristocracy in France, there was the guillotine. In recent years, there have been many more examples of shock events in places where the crowd looked like it may pull something off, but the tide turned. Tiananmen Square protests in Beijing occurred in 1989, the same time as a series of other protests around the end of the Soviet Union were taking place. China quickly understood that controlling the media was a key element here and started its response by first clearing all journalists out, expelling most foreign journalists from the country. It then responded with overwhelming military force and massive repression of the protestors, undertaking mass executions just over two weeks after the protests. Iran probably holds place of pride for having had a series of major situations of political unrest and protests (1999, 2009, 2019, 2022, 2025), and in almost all of them, the reaction of the state has been extremely swift and brutal, first using lethal force at the sites of protests, and then carrying out public executions of selected people they wanted to make examples of. But both China and Iran avoided executing high-profile student leaders both to avoid martyrdom and because students are younger and less prone to the fear of authority compared to family people or labour leaders. Russia (2012) and Turkey (2013) did not have the same exhibition of state violence through executions of even ordinary protestors, but were nonetheless effective at dismantling the protest movements. Both used targeted strategies to undermine protests. Russia used pre-emptive arrests, institutional undermining of potential protestors or powerful supporters of protestors, assassinations and lengthy prison sentences in dead end prisons. Beijing residents holding placards in English during a procession on May 18, 1989, in support to student hunger strikers who entered the sixth day at Tiananmen Square during the “Beijing Spring” movement. Credit: AFP. Turkey on the other hand is probably the closest example for what may work in India. Turkey did not see the same expansion of military into the cities, but a much bolder role played by their leader, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. Erdoğan came out in the open and spoke directly in rallies in both Ankara and Istanbul, framing the protests not as democratic critique, but as an existential threat to the religious and conservative aspirational classes. https://www.newsx.com/nx-news/parul-univ.text: Vadodara (Gujarat) [India], September 3: Parul University, Vadodara, in August 2026, organized two specialized programs on Ayurveda for 24 participants from Poland. These programs are a collaborative effort of the Faculty of Ayurveda and the Center for International Relations & Research (CIRR) and are based on the idea of promoting international collaboration within the framework of traditional Indian knowledge systems. The programs consisted of two-week Panchakarma Immersion Program (PIP) with 13 participants from Poland and three-week Ayurveda Practitioner Program (APP) with 11 practicing Ayurveda practitioners from Poland. The two programs provided an academic and experiential introduction to Ayurveda to international participants. They combined theoretical learning with practical demonstrations and hands-on exposure. The Panchakarma Immersion Program was developed to teach the basic principles and concepts of Ayurveda, an introduction to Panchakarma, techniques and procedures of Panchakarma and other Ayurvedic practices. For enhanced understanding of Ayurveda and its traditional approach to wellbeing, participants were engaged in practical demonstrations and experiential learning The Ayurveda Practitioner Program offered a total of 50+ hours of intensive learning experience, providing practicing Ayurveda professionals from Poland, direct interaction with Ayurveda doctors and Faculty Members of Parul University. The program included theoretical sessions, demonstrations, practical training and experiential learning on the principles and practices of Ayurved, Panchakarma and other Ayurvedic therapies. Speaking on the importance of International Ayurveda education, Dr. Komal Patel, Medical Director and Vice President, Parul University, quoted that “Ayurveda is an important part of India’s traditional knowledge system and its increasing international interest is a good avenue for academic and cultural exchange. We at Parul University are committed to offering a platform for international students to study and practice Ayurveda in both theoretical and practical aspects. Such programs not just strengthen global connections but also open pathways for knowledge exchange and deeper appreciation of India’s traditional healthcare wisdom.” The programs integrated academic learning with practical training, cultural immersion and international knowledge exchange, and thus gave participants the opportunity to experience Ayurveda within an Indian academic setting. Parul University still continues to promote global interaction in Ayurveda by participating in international initiatives of this nature, linking India’s traditional knowledge systems with learners and practitioners worldwide.
